Summary: The paper builds a benchmark from 100 OMIM phenotype entries (2-12 cited references each, stratified by creation era). One LLM drafts each entry from exactly the papers the curators cited, with the causal gene withheld. Only the generation strategy varies: direct long-context reading, an agentic curator with read and search tools, two extract-then-write pipelines (evidence graph, case table), recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, and three add-ons (second-hand evidence, reconciled case database, learned curation guide). The primary endpoint is coverage of fixed fact lists, split once from OMIM's allelic-variant paragraphs as deposited in ClinVar. Secondary measures are HPO synopsis F1, variant recall and precision, causal gene and inheritance, plus a claim-level audit against the cited papers. Main findings: (i) hiding the full text of the same papers drops coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (paired +43.7 points on 46 entries), and most missed facts are absent from the text supplied; (ii) on the 93 entries every strategy completed, the reading strategies sit at 47.2-49.1%, within or close to a measured replicate-noise half-width of 1.0 point; only the case table is clearly lower (-1.9), and the strategies separate observationally where more full text is readable; (iii) memory-based strategies reach about 15%; (iv) the audit caught all 60 planted single-fact errors and raised no flag on unaltered re-audit, but it checks fidelity to the source, not correctness. The authors also report measurement lessons, such as handling stopped replies symmetrically and fixing fact lists in advance.
Strengths: Well-controlled design. The sources, guards, audit and scoring are held fixed, so the generation strategy really is the only variable. Scoring against curators' own per-paper text, rather than open retrieval or QA benchmarks, is a useful framing that has not been done before for this task.

Unusually careful statistics and reporting: paired differences with bootstrap intervals, better/worse/tied counts, sign tests, a replicate-noise floor measured from three repeated runs on 30 entries, judge variation, an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 7), and completion treated as an outcome. Appendix Table 2 lists every experiment with its entry set and dropouts.

The within-paper full-text-hiding experiment (Figure 2) is a clean causal manipulation. The missed-fact attribution (Figure 3) and conveyed-fact provenance analysis convincingly show that the shortfall comes mainly from limited access rather than from the strategy.
Fact lists are fixed once, without sight of any draft, which removes a denominator confound common in atomic-fact evaluation. The paper shows that splitting afresh would inflate levels by 2-5 points.

Honest, explicit scoping. The paper reports negative results (recall-then-verify, learned guide, reconciliation), self-corrects a spurious 2.1-point deficit, and has a matched ablation that separates extraction effort from representation in the extract-then-write pipelines.
Includes a contamination check: memory-only performance by creation era, plus entries created after development (June-November 2026).
Weaknesses: Every judgement comes from one model family: it writes the drafts, splits the facts, judges coverage, audits claims, and attributes missed and conveyed facts. No human validated any fact list, coverage judgement or audit verdict, not even a small sample, and no second judge family was used. Replicate and judge variation measure precision, not validity. Self-preference bias (which the paper itself cites) could systematically favour some strategies, for example those whose phrasing is closer to the judge's own. For a benchmark paper whose main claims rest on these scores, a modest curator or expert validation on a sample is the most important missing piece.

The headline access result is largely expected, and the paper says so: curators wrote from full papers, and text mining is known to yield more from full text. The +43.7-point effect is well measured, but the conceptual contribution is limited. The second main finding, that reading strategies are close in this regime, is essentially a null result in a narrow regime: 2-12 references, inputs that fit one prompt, 19% full text, one model. Long-context, graph and agentic methods are expected to differ most in exactly the conditions not tested (large corpora, inputs beyond the context window, retrieval).

Generality to the ICLR audience is limited. The only model is a single proprietary model run through a CLI that exposes no temperature or seed, so other groups cannot reproduce the generations exactly. The strategies are the authors' own implementations, not published systems (GraphRAG, PaperQA2, STORM and others), so the comparison does not tell readers how existing methods rank.

The reference is narrow and indirect. Only variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs are scored, and the narrative phenotype text is unavailable. By the authors' own estimate, only 24% of a draft's statements have a counterpart in the reference, so most of each draft is checked only by a self-audit for fidelity. Coverage is therefore a partial and possibly strategy-biased view: extract-then-write pipelines that emphasise variants could be favoured or penalised in ways that do not reflect full entry quality.

The claim that strategies separate where more full text is readable rests on an observational split (21 entries in the top group, confounded with era and journal) and a 38-entry ablation in which two changes were made together. The attribution of the case table's gain to extraction effort is, as the authors admit, an inference. This claim is presented as a main result in the abstract and conclusion, but it is weakly supported.

The audit validation is limited. Planted errors are single rule-based value swaps (counts, zygosity, residues, inheritance), which are the easiest kind for a claim-level checker. Omissions, misattributed citations and subtler paraphrase errors are untested. The 0/60 re-audit result covers only paragraphs that had already passed, as the authors note.

Presentation is very dense and heavily hedged. Almost every sentence carries several parenthetical qualifiers (means over entries vs pooled over facts, n, intervals, b/w/t). This makes the abstract and Sections 4.1-4.2 hard to read and the takeaways hard to extract. The abstract alone runs to about 30 lines of numbers. Some figure-text pairings also need cross-checking: Figure 2 shows pooled coverage with the full-text bar after repair (77.4%), while the text leads with means over entries before repair (79.8%), and the paired-difference labels on the figure (+43.9) are the after-repair values.

Minor: Table 7 renders '<0.001' as '¡0.001' (font encoding). Figure 4 and Table 2 imply a fourth access stratum (1 entry) that is never explained. Table 1 reports variant precision for recall-then-verify on n=23 (100.0%), a value that is not meaningful at that n and needs a caveat in the main table.
Questions: Can you provide any human validation, even 100-200 facts or claims judged by a geneticist or an OMIM-style curator, for (a) the fact splitting, (b) present/partly/absent judgements and (c) audit verdicts? That would let readers estimate judge accuracy and any strategy-dependent bias.

Did you try a second judge model family (even on the 30-entry replicate subset) to check that the ordering and the closeness of reading strategies do not come from the judge sharing the generator's family?

How do the reading strategies compare when inputs exceed one prompt? The 30-75-reference tier has about ten comparable entries. Is there any plan to scale it, given that this is where graph and agentic designs are expected to matter?
In the matched ablation, can you separate the two changes (extraction effort vs writer-chosen synopsis terms and inheritance) with an additional arm, rather than inferring the cause?
What is the single entry in the fourth access stratum (Table 2: 46/25/21/1)?

How sensitive is the primary endpoint to the half credit given for 'partly present'? Table 5 reports full-only coverage. Do the paired differences and their intervals change when partial credit is dropped?
Why were published systems such as PaperQA2 and GraphRAG not run as additional strategies under the same guards? Even one would anchor the implementations to the literature.
Limitations: The paper's limitations section is thorough and candid: one model family, no human validation, a narrow reference, the reference list given to every strategy, open-access text only without supplements, a small post-development sample, and stopped replies.

Not sufficiently emphasised: the closeness of strategies may partly reflect the judge's own family, and the results may not transfer to settings with retrieval or larger corpora, where design choices are expected to matter most.
Thought: A careful, honest and statistically disciplined benchmark study, and better controlled than most LLM-for-curation papers. The core problems: every measurement is a self-judgement by one model family with zero human validation; the headline finding (full text beats abstracts) is expected; the strategy comparison is a null within a narrow regime where differences would not be expected; and the 'separation' claim is observational or rests on a confounded ablation. Generality for ICLR is limited (one proprietary model, in-house implementations, a niche genetics task). The prose is dense to the point of hurting readability. Strong rigor, modest significance, missing validity check: leaning reject, but a human-validation sample plus a second judge family could move it to a weak accept.
